items.title: Follow the money or follow the flag? Politics clouds port investment
items.original_title: Follow the money or follow the flag? Politics clouds port investment
items.summary: In the seven years since TOC Americas last took place in Cartagena, global laden container volumes have slipped about 10% below where they would have been without the multiple disruptions that have hit the industry since 2018, according to Dinesh Sharma, director at Drewry Maritime Advisors. Sharma’s research measured growth from 2018 against forecasts of where the industry had imagined it would be today last time they met in Cartagena. Predicting the future, he said, was and is not easy. Transshipment hubs grew by about 6% a year on average over that period, against roughly 3% for gateway ports and 1.5% for the underlying economies they serve. The inefficiency, he said, is no longer contained at the big transshipment hubs: it is flowing through to gateways too, leaving Latin America’s overall throughput an estimated 2–3% below his 2018 projection. Washington’s growing interest in the region’s infrastructure raises the odds that port decisions get caught up in politics rather than commercial logic.

items.title: Imported iron ore margins narrow to 9.62 yuan/mt on higher brand premiums
items.original_title: Imported iron ore margins narrow to 9.62 yuan/mt on higher brand premiums
items.summary: The average margin on imported iron ore narrowed to 9.62 yuan/mt today from 11.52 yuan/mt, driven mainly by higher premiums on some brands alongside weaker spot prices. On the supply side, BHP’s Q1 FY2027 report showed Western Australia Iron Ore (WAIO) production at 71.91 million mt on a 100% basis, up 2.4% year-on-year, with full-year guidance unchanged at 286-298 million mt. Lump accounted for 27.9% of WAIO sales, the lowest in five quarters. On freight, SMM data showed the Australia-China route up 0.49/mt week-on-week at 11.91/mt on 19 October, while the Brazil-China route eased to 30.46/mt. The net change in CFR costs was limited. On the demand side, mills remain lossmaking and restocking is still on a just-in-need basis, with port inventories building again last week. Futures lost upward momentum after yesterday’s rebound and spot prices edged lower. Iron ore prices are likely to stay range-bound in the near term with limited upside, and import margins are expected to hold in modest positive territory. Source: SMM

items.title: European gas rallies on Persian gulf disruption pressure; Hot UK Inflation dents
items.original_title: European gas rallies on Persian gulf disruption pressure; Hot UK Inflation dents
items.summary: European wholesale natural gas prices surged on Wednesday, with both major regional benchmarks gaining over 3% as hotter-than-expected British inflation data and ongoing Persian Gulf energy disruptions heightened anxieties over winter fuel adequacy. The benchmark Dutch TTF front-month contract rose 3.1% to trade at 87.95 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh). In Great Britain, the equivalent NBP natural gas futures contract similarly advanced 3.2% to 216.57 pence per therm, with both contracts holding near their highest levels since late 2022. Wednesday’s gas rally coincided with fresh macroeconomic data highlighting the acute economic toll of elevated energy import costs on the British economy. Official figures showed Britain’s annual consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and exceeding market consensus. Lacking large-scale long-term gas storage infrastructure, the UK relies heavily on real-time imports of pipeline gas and Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) cargoes to meet domestic power generation and home heating needs. The European benchmark remains up approximately 210% year-to-date. With maritime strikes and transit friction restricting LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz – keeping Middle Eastern deliveries to Europe nearly 80% below year-ago levels—European utilities face intense competition from Asian buyers for uncommitted Atlantic basin cargoes.

items.original_title: IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Crude oil tanker Odessa, carrying UAE crude after passing through the Strait of Hormuz with its Automatic Identification System transponder turned off, navigates the waters at Daesan port, where it is expected to discharge crude oil, in Seosan, South Korea, May 8, 2026. REUTERS/Kim Soo-hyeon/File Photo The cost of shipping crude oil from the Middle East Gulf to Asia has surged to more than $37 per barrel, over five times prewar levels, as an increasingly complex shipping network keeps oil flowing despite escalating Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Energy Agency. The extraordinary increase comes as Persian Gulf oil exports have actually surpassed prewar levels, highlighting the steep price of maintaining energy flows through one of the world’s most dangerous shipping corridors. According to The Wall Street Journal , citing vessel-tracking data from Kpler, Middle East oil shipments averaged more than 24 million barrels per day in the week ending October 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels per day. In a separate analysis published Wednesday , the IEA said tanker rates reached historic highs in September and continued climbing into October, with the cost of transporting crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia exceeding $37 per barrel by mid-month.

items.title: Nearly two-thirds of Far East-Europe capacity now back to Suez Canal
items.original_title: Nearly two-thirds of Far East-Europe capacity now back to Suez Canal
items.summary: Some 63% of the ocean capacity deployed between the Far East and Europe has returned to the Red Sea, following three years of detours, but some operators are hedging against renewed disruption by maintaining several Cape of Good Hope routes. Having surveyed the 10 largest carrier networks over the past month, Alphaliner found vessels on 24 of the 46 direct Far East–Europe services were transiting the Red Sea, accounting for 70% of deployed capacity on Far East-Mediterranean routes. On the Far East-North Europe trades, the number was a little lower, 58%, with containers moving between the Far East and Europe via Suez now topping 5.5m teu, of the possible 8.7m teu available to the trades – CMA CGM alone accounting for 1.3m of this. However, the Suez return remains something of a mixed bag, with multiple services opting to transit the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait on outbound routes to Europe, but electing to sail around the Cape on return journeys. Of the 10 carriers surveyed, five confirmed they had resumed Red Sea transits over the past month, that number set to climb to eight after Premier Alliance partners HMM, ONE, and Yang Ming all announced a return to the waterway.

items.original_title: Airfreight in Africa booming, thanks to disrupted ocean shipping services
items.summary: African airfreight is seeing something of a boom from the disruption in ocean freight across the Middle East, but forwarders remain sceptical as to whether it will provoke long-term structural benefits. Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express’s Sub-Saharan Africa operations, told The Loadstar the shift from ocean services had left airfreight the only viable alternative to keep goods moving. “When people run into trouble from a seafreight point of view, the alternative becomes airfreight, becomes express, and that is a notable trend across African airfreight’s growth momentum at the moment,” Mr Heymans told The Loadstar . For DHL Express, the timing has proved particularly useful, coinciding with the launch of its Heavy Weight Express service, allowing its customers to ship consignments of up to 3,000kg, with individual pieces of up to 1,000kg. Expanding beyond smaller parcels, the new service is designed for automotive, energy, engineering, machinery, and pharmaceuticals, Mr Heymans noting the significant cost implications delays place on these sectors. “The timing of the launch worked out quite well, which makes the conversation a lot easier, and a lot more comfortable for those customers seeking these sorts of services,” explained Mr Heymans.

items.title: AG Seville wins 25-year port shipyard concession with $11m investment plan
items.original_title: AG Seville wins 25-year port shipyard concession with $11m investment plan
items.summary: AG Seville Shipyard has won the competition to continue operating the ship repair facilities at Spain’s Port of Seville, clearing an important hurdle for a proposed €10m ($11.2m) investment programme. Seville Port Authority’s board approved the selection of AG Seville Shipyard on October 20, allowing the company to retain its position at the former Astilleros del Guadalquivir facilities. The operator’s existing concession expires in December.The new concession will cover approximately 22,000 sq m of port land and infrastructure, including the dry dock, the southern section of the Muelle de Armamento and a disused slipway. The concession can run for up to 25 years, although final administrative approval is still required before the new agreement becomes effective. AG Seville Shipyard faced competition for the facilities from Spanish maritime group Boluda, which had also expressed interest in taking over the site. The successful operator has controlled part of the former Seville shipyard since 2017, developing ship repair and maintenance operations at facilities that had suffered years of decline following the collapse of the former public shipyard. The larger €10m programme is AG Seville’s proposed investment plan, rather than an amount separately confirmed as contractually committed in the latest announcement. The port authority also approved an additional €4.2m ($4.7m) for improvements to Seville’s port free zone.

Crude was also buoyed by industry data pointing to a big draw in U.S. oil inventories, which further underscored rapidly tightening market conditions in the world’s biggest fuel consumer. President Donald Trump called for no attacks on Iran before the November 3 U.S. oil inventories fall sharply- API Adding to concerns over stretched supplies, data from the American Petroleum Institute showed U.S. Oil inventories fell 4.93 million barrels in the week to October 16, much more than expectations for a 1.3 million barrel draw. The API data usually heralds a similar print from official inventory data, which is due later on Wednesday. The outsized inventory draws also come with the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve at its lowest level in 44 years, following months of emergency releases to tide over global oil supply disruptions.

This marked the first green methanol refueling operation for a Ro-Ro vessel in Guangdong, signifying a key step forward for the Nansha Automobile Terminal of Guangzhou Port in upgrading its green and low-carbon shipping services and in building a global export channel for domestic automobiles. The operation helps establish the Guangzhou-based port as the world’s first port to achieve green methanol refueling operations for three types of clean energy-powered vessels — container ships, bulk carriers and automobile Ro-Ro ships, according to the port operator. The CM Guangzhou vessel, with a design capacity of 7,800 standard car units, is a new generation of large green Ro-Ro ships and the first methanol dual-fuel Ro-Ro ship to dock at the Nansha Automobile Terminal. The supply of green marine fuel in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area has progressed from single-ship pilot projects to a stage of multi-ship type and full-scenario coverage, according to Li Guanjie, deputy general manager of the bonded business division of China Shipping and Sinopec Suppliers Co Ltd.

items.summary: Monaco-based shipowner Gestion Maritime is moving into the ultramax segment with an order for three 64,000 dwt bulk carriers at China’s Nantong Xiangyu Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering. The Danilo Fumarola-led company has booked the trio for delivery between late 2028 and early 2029, expanding beyond its traditional panamax and kamsarmax fleet. The vessels are costing in the low $30m range apiece, putting the overall investment at more than $90m. Gestion Maritime currently operates six panamax and kamsarmax bulkers and has recently trimmed its fleet through asset sales. The latest investment will bring smaller and more modern tonnage into a portfolio built largely around Japanese- and South Korean-built ships. The company, whose roots date back to 1908 and the Corrado shipping family, has traditionally pursued an asset trading strategy, buying ships when values ease and disposing of tonnage during stronger markets. In 2019, it exited the product tanker sector by selling two 2015-built MR tankers to Hafnia interests for $31m each, returning its focus to dry bulk. The newbuilding deal adds another international owner to Nantong Xiangyu’s growing customer base. The Chinese shipbuilder marked the delivery of its 100th ultramax bulker in July and has continued to attract orders for the 63,500 to 64,000 dwt segment.

items.title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
items.original_title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
items.summary: Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle linking Jebel Ali in Dubai with Umm Qasr, Iraq’s principal container gateway. The first sailing was scheduled to depart Jebel Ali yesterday, arriving in Umm Qasr two days later. Iraq’s transport ministry has described the initiative as the national carrier’s first regular Gulf operation since the mid-1960s. The relaunch comes as Iraqi container supply chains have been radically reshaped since the Hormuz shipping crisis erupted at the end of February. According to the Jordan Shipping Association, Aqaba handled 37,182 Iraq-bound transit containers during the first seven months of 2026, compared with just 3,599 during the corresponding period last year, a 933% increase. Hapag-Lloyd outlined a routing in July whereby containers are discharged at Khorfakkan, outside the Strait of Hormuz, before being trucked across the UAE to Sharjah or Jebel Ali and transferred onto third-party feeder vessels serving Iraq and other upper Gulf destinations.

items.title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
items.original_title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
items.summary: Ports and terminals are no strangers to reinvention. Over the past 50 years, the industry has managed and adapted to the shift to containerization and ever-larger vessels, the move from paper manifests to electronic messaging and transactions, and the subsequent evolution to system-to-system integration with other parties in the shipping industries. But many port functions still run on clipboards, radio calls, or the gut instincts of a planner, who has watched the yard fill up and empty thousands of times. To assess how far the industry has come, BCG and TIC4.0 (an international nonprofit association of terminal operators and equipment and solution providers dedicated to the creation and promotion of digital standards for the cargo-handling industry) surveyed more than 100 leaders from across the container ports and terminals ecosystem. On average, those we surveyed are already using or exploring the top 16 of the 43 use cases we assessed, from extracting data from shipping documents (62%) to predicting when a crane or straddle carrier will fail (48%). Survey Demographics In August 2026, BCG and the Terminal Industry Committee 4.0 (TIC4.0) surveyed the port and terminal ecosystem on the adoption of AI and generative AI, to establish where the industry sees the opportunity and where it sees the risk.

Since 2023, MPA and CCS have worked with local research and industry partners on projects ranging from the use of B100 biofuel on harbour craft to the evaluation, testing and verification for smart ships. Under the renewed agreement, MPA and CCS will expand their collaboration on research and development in decarbonisation, including green fuel value chain, marine electrification and energy efficiency technologies for vessels. Both organisations will also deepen collaboration on digital and smart ship initiatives, such as digital testing and risk assessment for autonomous vessels, to support research and innovation in the maritime sector. Both organisations will also collaborate to support talent development through programmes such as the MPA Global Internship Awards, the MaritimeONE Scholarship Programme and internships, as well as attachments which will provide students and aspiring maritime professionals with exposure to international maritime companies and industry practices.

items.title: ESI 2.0 prompts ports to rethink environmental incentive schemes
items.original_title: ESI 2.0 prompts ports to rethink environmental incentive schemes
items.summary: The updated Environmental Ship Index (ESI 2.0) is prompting ports to review how they reward better environmental performance, as the new methodology brings vessel scoring more closely in line with the environmental priorities shaping shipping today. Developed and owned by IAPH and administered globally by OceanScore, ESI provides ports with a framework for identifying and incentivising vessels that perform beyond environmental standards. ESI 2.0 updates this framework to reflect developments in regulation, technology and vessel operations, with increased recognition of areas including energy use, greenhouse gas performance, innovation and electrification. ESI 2.0 reflects the priorities of shipping today As shipping adopts cleaner fuels, electrification and new emissions-reduction technologies, the way environmental performance is measured also needs to evolve. Port of Aarhus turns the new methodology into action To understand the impact of ESI 2.0, OceanScore analysed Port of Aarhus’ 2025 vessel calls and how its existing incentive scheme would perform under the updated methodology. Keeping incentives effective as shipping evolves The Aarhus example demonstrates how ports can respond to changes in environmental performance measurement while keeping their incentive schemes relevant to the vessels they serve. “ESI 2.0 reflects how environmental priorities in shipping are evolving, and the Aarhus example shows how ports can translate that into practical incentives,” says Thomas Smith, Head of Cargo Solutions at OceanScore.

items.title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.original_title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.summary: Shipping’s drive to digitalise risks slowing itself down as fragmented software, weak digital training and growing pressure to adopt artificial intelligence add complexity to operational and commercial decisions, according to OrbitMI. OrbitMI warns that the sector is entering a period of ‘digital fatigue’: growing scepticism and frustration when technology fails to deliver the promised simplicity or measurable productivity and performance improvement gains. After years of adding platforms and bolt-on applications, many teams still transfer data manually, work across separate dashboards and adapt established processes to generic interfaces. Research by Thetius and Marcura found that 82% of maritime professionals believe AI can improve efficiency and 81% are running pilots, but only 11% have the policies and governance needed to scale it. Two-thirds are concerned that overreliance on AI could erode human judgement, while 69% worry it may miss critical red flags in contracts or voyage planning. What users need are tools that are truly collaborative and are fully integrated in their workflows; always present but never intrusive. OrbitMI has been investing in this approach through the acquisition of AI specialist AuQub and maritime advisory and voyage optimisation business Gale Force, alongside the expansion of its maritime, product and technology leadership over the past 18 months.

items.original_title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
items.summary: Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident around bunkering, crew changes and stores, where technical departments can still be managing substantial sums through spreadsheets and email. “Husbandry calls have never carried the same profit and loss visibility as commercial port calls,” Malaxianakis tells Maritime CEO. For Malaxianakis, who worked in disbursement departments at Thenamaris and Product Shipping & Trading before founding HarborLab in 2020, the problem is less about a lack of attention from technical managers than the tools available to them. “One data point from our analysis makes the structural difference concrete: 75% of technical managers in APAC still manage husbandry bills in Excel today, compared with 40% in EMEA,” he says. The HarborLab-managed vessels generated $220,000 in savings compared with $70,000 on the other half. The system also picks up incorrect and duplicated charges, with the company then taking discrepancies back to agents in an effort to turn the finding into a credit. Behind that sits a database built from more than 40,000 port calls across over 1,400 ports.

This shipment is the 19th case of crude transport via the Red Sea since the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz began at the end of February. South Korean oil tankers had originally, from April, loaded crude at Yanbu Port on the Red Sea and entered South Korea via the southern Bab el-Mandeb Strait. As the closure of the Strait of Hormuz becomes prolonged, detour shipments to secure domestic energy supply are expected to continue for the time being. So far, a total of 19 South Korean vessels have transported crude oil through the Red Sea. The government said it is continuously monitoring the safe operation of vessels and managing the situation to prevent disruptions in crude oil supply.

items.summary: A satellite image of side-by-side ships at sea, off the coast of Sohar, Oman, June 9, 2026. SPOT © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS/Handout via REUTERS Maritime data provider Kpler has reached an agreement with Airbus to expand its ability to track vessels that disappear from conventional ship-tracking systems, adding daily satellite imagery to help identify ships operating without reliable Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. The agreement, announced Tuesday , will integrate imagery from Airbus’s SPOT Earth observation satellites with Kpler’s existing vessel-tracking network, allowing analysts to detect ships independently of their reported AIS positions. The service will use high-resolution satellite imagery, with a resolution of 1.5 meters and a 60-kilometer swath, combined with artificial intelligence to identify vessels at sea and in port. The technology is intended to address a growing challenge for maritime tracking: determining whether a vessel has deliberately switched off or manipulated its AIS signal, or whether its reported position has been affected by interference with satellite navigation systems. By comparing AIS data with independently captured satellite imagery, Kpler says it can better distinguish between the two. items.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard. In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January 2025, had imposed a substantially greater administrative workload on shipowners and regulators than initially anticipated. The 22-page report identifies difficulties with reporting deadlines, fuel certification, emissions calculations and compliance pooling arrangements. The Chamber wants the UK government to establish a fully tested ship-level monitoring and reporting system before introducing compliance obligations. Peter Aylott, the Chamber’s director of policy, said the government had an opportunity to learn from the EU’s experience rather than create another regulatory system that increased costs and complexity. The paper also calls for close alignment with emerging International Maritime Organization requirements to avoid duplicate certification, reporting and verification obligations. The intervention comes as the Department for Transport prepares to consult on a domestic maritime fuel standard, with the consultation expected later this year. Britain’s maritime decarbonisation strategy, unveiled in March 2025, targets a 30% reduction in domestic shipping’s lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, rising to 80% by 2040 and zero by 2050, against a 2008 baseline.

items.summary: South Asian LNG markets have absorbed one of the most severe supply shocks in the history of the global gas trade, as the war in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz cut off Qatari and UAE LNG flows to a region that had made itself critically dependent on them. LNG demand across South Asia, which had been projected to grow by 2.7 million tonnes (Mt), or 7%, in 2026, is now expected to decline by around 6 Mt and the outlook beyond 2026 has been materially downgraded, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest analysis. In 2025, nearly 90% of Qatari and UAE LNG shipments through the Strait were destined for Asia, making the region the most affected. The vessels, Pacific Sentinel and Pacific Sunstone , have each been fitted with three 22-metre suction sails, making them the first ships in the EPS fleet to adopt wind-assisted propulsion. The financing model builds on earlier trials involving GCMD and EPS aboard Pacific Sentinel , during which researchers collected 276m data points over four months of trading in the Americas between May and September 2025. The analysis examined 203 valid sail on-off transitions to isolate the technology’s impact on fuel consumption from changing operating conditions. items.summary: The chief officer of a Portuguese-flagged bulk carrier is missing after being swept overboard during a dramatic operation that rescued all 28 seafarers from a burning 11,800 teu containership in the South Atlantic. The Seaspan-owned, Hapag-Lloyd-chartered containership had suffered a serious fire while sailing from Singapore towards Santos, Brazil. The Aeolian Arrow launched its rescue boat in heavy seas, recovering 19 crew members from a lifeboat and another nine from a life raft. However, as the bulker’s rescue boat was being recovered, its chief officer fell into the sea. Portugal’s Maritime Accident Investigation Office (GAMA) said the officer was initially spotted alive, but repeated attempts to recover him were unsuccessful before he disappeared from sight. The 330 m Espirito Santo Express , built in 2018 and capable of carrying approximately 11,900 teu, was subsequently left abandoned and drifting in the South Atlantic. Hapag-Lloyd and fellow service operator Ocean Network Express have confirmed the containership’s crew survived, while warning that the impact on cargo and vessel operations remains under assessment.

items.summary: The seaborne trade in spodumene, a lithium-bearing mineral essential for battery production, is emerging as one of dry bulk shipping’s fastest-growing niche cargoes, with volumes more than tripling over the past five years. New research from Greek shipbroker Ursa Shipbrokers shows global shipments reached 4.04m tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, up 11.9% year-on-year and a record for the period. Annual shipments have climbed from just 1.58m tonnes in 2020 to 5.08m tonnes last year, reflecting the rapid expansion of lithium mining and growing demand from electric vehicle manufacturers and battery storage projects. Australia dominates the trade, accounting for 81% of shipments during the first nine months of this year, equivalent to 3.26m tonnes. China remains overwhelmingly the principal destination, receiving 88% of global seaborne spodumene cargoes, equivalent to 3.56m tonnes, reflecting its dominant position in lithium refining and battery manufacturing. Ultramaxes accounted for 39.6% of vessel deadweight employed in spodumene shipments this year, with handysizes representing a further 46%. New trading routes are also developing as African lithium production expands. Last week, Kodal Minerals confirmed that a fifth shipment of approximately 17,400 tonnes of spodumene concentrate had departed the Ivory Coast’s port of San Pedro in September, carrying material from its Bougouni mine in Mali to China.

items.original_title: Northern Sea Route smashes shipping records again
items.summary: Shipping along Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) has already broken last year’s transit record. New figures from Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) show 104 confirmed transits by September 30, surpassing the 103 recorded during the whole of 2025 and 97 in 2024. Estimated transit cargo reached 3.7m tonnes, up 15% on the whole of last year, while the combined deadweight of vessels using the route increased 26% to 7.8m dwt. CHNL identified another 45 potential transits already underway or within the route at the end of September, suggesting the season could approach 150 voyages and more than 4.5m tonnes of cargo. Four direct Asia-Europe voyages had been completed by September 30, compared with just one during the whole of last year. Russian oil exports through the NSR have climbed nearly 50% this year, with approximately 20m barrels shipped to Asia between July and mid-October. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal and Black Sea has made the expensive and potentially hazardous Arctic passage increasingly attractive. Russian LNG shipments are also contributing to traffic growth, with CHNL recording four eastbound LNG cargoes totalling approximately 300,000 tonnes.

UK-based bunker supplier Avenir LNG has launched the second of two 20,000-cbm LNG bunker vessels it ordered from a Chinese shipyard, and expects it to join its fleet next year. items.title: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action
items.original_title: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action
items.summary: InterManager has called for urgent industry action on enclosed space safety after its latest research highlighted persistent failures in procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention. The organisation has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents over the past 30 years, between 1996 and 2026, across tankers, bulkers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. Its latest seafarer survey identifies a recurring gap between safety procedures and operational reality onboard. InterManager says this must now be enhanced to deliver competence, rather than just training, particularly as enclosed space entry training is being considered as part of the current review of STW requirements, with the International Chamber of Shipping leading industry input. InterManager will explore the survey findings and wider enclosed space safety concerns during a webinar, run in conjunction with The Nautical Institute, on 27 October 2026 at 10am GMT. The webinar will bring together industry experts, Captain Pradeep Chawla, CEO of Marie Pals, Captain Garry Hallett from InterManager and Richard Cowburn, human factors specialist, to discuss where the industry stands now on enclosed space safety, how seafarers and shore-based stakeholders feel about current practice, and what practical action is needed next.

In 2025, the Group adopted a decarbonisation pathway covering its operations and value chain, with 139 initiatives planned between 2025 and 2050. The Group continued to advance its decarbonisation journey as the business grew robustly in 2025, reducing the total emissions intensity of our business per AED 1 million of revenue by 6% from 2024 levels through greater efficiencies and the use of solar and alternative energy.

items.title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.original_title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.summary: Shipping companies need to pay as much attention to managing crew turnover as they do to retaining seafarers if they are to maintain safe and efficient vessel operations, according to Henrik Jensen, founder and CEO of Danica Crewing Specialists. Speaking ahead of this week’s Crew Connect Global 2026 in Manila (20-22 October), Mr Jensen warned that while retaining experienced seafarers remains a priority, changing attitudes towards employment mean shipowners and managers must accept that some crew turnover is inevitable and be better prepared to manage it. “Having a stable crew pool makes a significant difference to the safe and efficient operation of a vessel. We also need to think about how we manage these changes when they happen.” Mr Jensen explained that traditional retention strategies, including competitive salaries, bonuses, insurance, pensions and promotion opportunities, have largely been built around the expectations of older generations, who tend to value stability and long-term employment. Mr Jensen believes shipping companies should focus on making it easier for new crew members to familiarise themselves with onboard equipment, procedures and working practices.

He also highlighted the importance of strong tripartism to enable PSA’s management team, the unions and the workers to work together in a “relationship of trust” to build a “disciplined and skilled workforce”. Mr Lee was speaking at a dinner celebration for the 80th anniversary of the Singapore Port Workers Union (SPWU), which represents PSA employees. But other ports in the region are making progress digitalising and automating too,” said Mr Lee, citing Shanghai’s Yangshan port as an example. “Each required close coordination between port management and the unions – to help workers accept radical changes in their work processes, to upgrade themselves as their roles changed, and then safely and successfully adopt new ways of working, sometimes in new places.” There were also many port moves – including to Keppel, Brani, Pasir Panjang and Tuas Port – that needed workers to adjust to different work environments and commuting arrangements.

items.title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.original_title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.summary: In an industry where a position list is a competitive weapon, the question is no longer just how to comply—but where carbon decisions are made and who controls the data behind them, said Argyris Zafeiropoulos, principal advisor at Resilience & Compliance Advisory. With the EU Emissions Trading System fully phased into shipping and FuelEU Maritime tightening year by year, carbon is now a line item in every fixture. On a single laden Aframax voyage from the Gulf to Rotterdam, the FuelEU penalty alone climbs to about €246,000 ($276,000) by 2040 — same ship, same route, same fuel. Far less attention goes to a quieter question: where are these carbon decisions actually made, and who can see the data behind them? On that voyage, ETS and FuelEU together come to about €104,000 ($116,600) at an €81 ($91) allowance price — roughly one euro ($1.12) on every tonne of a 100,000-tonne cargo, rising to about €1.36 ($1.53) by 2030. In commodity trades, the choice between CIF and FOB helps decide who absorbs it. Carbon has moved beyond the charter party and into the commodity contract. Shipping has always rewarded those who control their critical assets — ships, cargo relationships, market intelligence and commercial judgement.

items.original_title: Oil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: Iran’s Guards
items.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Monday an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway. Iran seized control of the strait after war broke out against the United States and Israel late February, choking off the vital shipping route which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil. The Islamic republic has demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. “An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room,” Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying. The tanker was travelling in the strait’s “unauthorized southern route” and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said. It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines. The Guards’ naval commander Admiral Ali Ozmaei warned this week that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile.” The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports in response to Tehran’s blockade on the waterway. Maersk said the new service was designed to complement its other Asia-Europe strings as well as flows from Asia to West Africa and South America with its west Mediterranean hubs taking on more relay transhipment responsibilities. items.summary: Would a carrier really design its Asia-Europe network around shaving marginal ETS dollars, which it can recoup through surcharges anyway? In short, carriers did redesign for the ETS – though not around the ETS alone. Carriers have redesigned Asia–Europe loops to cut their exposure, and they were right to. A few months ago, the EU ETS Observatory published a report stating that UK volume growth was a direct result of shippers seeking to minimise the EU-ETS charges – bullocks, if you ask me. The first is above – carriers optimised their networks within the rules, as they were entitled to, and importers were spared hundreds of millions of euros a year: the Observatory puts the allowances not collected at the three UK ports alone at about €316m. It removes the carbon price from the Asia leg, the longest of the voyage, and with it any ETS reason to slow down or burn a bio-blend there. The commission’s carbon market report found about 5% of national ETS revenue went to industrial decarbonisation, and only France and Estonia ringfence a share for shipping. Its July proposal would create a reserve of up to 110m allowances from 2028 to 2040, covering 55%–90% of the price gap for sustainable fuels and zero-emission propulsion.

The first product, Shipbuilding Project Credit Risk Insurance Policy, has been developed by state-owned export credit insurer ECGC and will cover shipbuilding contracts for overseas owners. The second, Business Credit Shield Policy–Shipbuilders, has been developed by New India Assurance and targets domestic shipbuilding projects. The initiative addresses one of the financial risks facing shipbuilders, particularly on large contracts where construction can take several years and payments are tied to milestones. Delayed instalments or buyer defaults can leave yards exposed to substantial working capital requirements while vessels remain under construction. The two products were introduced under India’s $2.1bn shipbuilding development scheme, part of a wider maritime investment package approved by the government in September 2025. The roughly $152m allocation is part of that existing programme. India has been stepping up financial support for its shipbuilding industry as it seeks to expand domestic construction capacity and attract more international orders.

A study published by European Community Shipowners’ Associations (ECSA) estimates that the proposed Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism needs at least 330m allowances, compared with the 110m currently envisaged by the European Commission. The association puts the required support at around €30bn ($33.6bn), aimed at narrowing the cost gap between conventional marine fuels and cleaner alternatives. The proposal forms part of the ongoing revision of the EU ETS and remains subject to approval by the European Parliament and Council. With the phase-in period completed, shipping companies must surrender allowances covering 100% of their emissions falling within the ETS framework from the 2026 emissions year. The association estimates that shipowners purchase roughly 90m allowances annually. At an illustrative carbon price of €100 per allowance, that would represent an annual outlay of approximately €9bn ($10.1bn). ECSA argues that the proposed reserve, covering 2028 to 2040, would meet only about one-third of the industry’s estimated requirements. The intervention comes as shipowners weigh increasing carbon compliance costs against the substantial premiums associated with alternative fuels, fleet upgrades and new propulsion systems.
